item.title: H-1B visa delays and Trump's rules force tech workers to leave US
item.description: Uncertainty over H-1B rules and permanent residency is prompting some highly skilled Indian professionals to consider leaving the US, despite strong jobs and career prospects in its technology sector ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Francesca Maglione and Alicia A. Caldwell Yash Sharma decided last month that he’s had enough of the US. The 36-year-old Google software engineer from India says halfway through Donald Trump’s second term, the constant rule changes around visas for highly skilled immigrants, the unknowns they create and the slim odds of him becoming a citizen have all become too much. Sharma, who has had an H-1B visa for six years, says it’s become hard to focus at work. And while he loves his life in San Francisco and working at the epicenter of tech and AI, he feels like he’s run out of options to gain permanent residency and build a life here.  The US feels like a “golden prison,” Sharma said. He plans to move to the UK next month, even though he doesn’t have a job there, because he was offered a visa with a clear path to staying in the country for the long term. This month’s midterm elections delivered a rebuke of Trump’s immigration crackdown, helping Democrats win control of Congress and prompting the president to acknowledge that his administration may have been “too tough” in deporting people who had jobs.  But less acknowledged has been the administration’s reshaping of visa rules that for years have channeled graduates and highly skilled employees into the workforce. The newly empowered opposition won’t have an easy time reversing Trump’s rule changes, which have effectively dismantled an immigration system that helped make America a destination for the world’s best engineers and researchers. Just this week, the Labor Department proposed tighter rules for companies seeking to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency. Some of the biggest US companies are giving up on the idea anything will change soon. International Business Machines Corp. is ending US visa sponsorships for most jobs in its largest division, leaving affected employees to transfer outside the US or plan on leaving the company by year-end. Payments company Flywire Corp. is weighing whether to put more hiring and development work overseas, while Microsoft Corp., Adobe Inc. and a handful of IT outsourcing firms have been barred from a key green-card sponsorship program as federal officials probe their practices. The Trump administration says workers and employers have abused the immigration system for years, moving it away from its origins as a way to get highly specialized talent into the country on a temporary basis into a sprawling behemoth that’s resulted in lower pay for Americans.  Research into the question of how immigrants affect wages has shown mixed results. But a recently released study by a Harvard University economist who served on Trump’s Council of Economic Advisers found skilled immigration leads to lower pay for college-educated US workers, particularly in scientific fields. Trump’s appointment this month of Stephen Miller as chief of staff gives the longtime advocate of reducing all forms of immigration greater authority, while investigations into employers’ green-card sponsorships, announced last month by Vice President JD Vance, have added to the pressure. “It’s a quiet dismantling of employment-based immigration,” said Angelo Paparelli, an immigration attorney and partner at Vialto Law. There’s a growing sense that the friction and unpredictability are the new normal for the US immigration system. That’s changing assumptions about the future of the US economy and forcing businesses to plan for a world in which they may not be able to bring top talent to work in their US headquarters.  “Economies of scale are tricky things. It’s a bit like a reputation: it can take years to build and no time to utterly destroy it,” said Scott Corley, executive director of Compete America, a coalition of major US technology and high-skilled professional employers.  Sharma says he’s felt discouraged about the chances he’d ever be able to convert his temporary visa into permanent residency given a huge backlog for Indian nationals. He hasn’t left the country in a year and a half, concerned he might not be able to get back in. That’s meant missing out on family visits, work conferences and trips with friends. Global Talent He sought another path to permanent residency and more stability by applying for an “extraordinary ability” visa, given to people with standout talent in their field, but was rejected after months of waiting. The uncertainly led Sharma to consider a life outside the US. He applied for a Global Talent visa from the UK and was approved, allowing him to move to the UK without a job and begin looking for work. He says the US election results haven’t dissuaded him from the plan. “I’ve seen various administrations, and to me it’s clear that there will be no actual change to the law,” he said. And even if things returned to how they were before, the difficulty of getting permanent residency would still weigh on him. “That normal still sucks,” he said.  Trump’s broad immigration crackdown started almost immediately after he took office. After campaigning on a pledge to end illegal immigration, the dragnet expanded to include narrowing paths for legal immigration, adding new regulations and steep fees.  By September last year, the popular H-1B visa program for high-skilled foreign workers became a focus, first with a presidential proclamation requiring a $100,000 payment for certain prospective job candidates outside the US. In August, despite a court order blocking that original payment, the administration moved to impose a separate $103,000 fee for new H-1B visa applications.Legal ChallengesMany of Trump’s policy changes are facing legal challenges, but the chaos and confusion are difficult for companies and workers to navigate. Swapnil Deshpande, who works as a senior data analyst at a major US tech firm, said that the constant changes in immigration policy have made it hard to envision a stable future in the US. The Indian national arrived in 2018 to pursue a master’s degree at Northeastern University and has been working in New York for almost six years. Every day he wakes up feeling like it could be his last in the US. He said two years ago, he had somewhat of a plan of how his next five years would go. Maybe he would start a family, buy a home and establish a life here. But in the last two years, that plan has become blurry. “Me and my wife both wanted to get a house and start a journey, but now the next question for us is like, ‘What’s going to happen next month or next day? Where will we land? What is really there for us?’” he said. “Is the uncertainty, stress, unpredictability really worth it?” Employers are also rethinking how they hire some of the most highly sought-after foreign workers.  IBM told employees this month that it would stop sponsoring foreign workers for most jobs in its consulting division, according to a document shared with managers that Bloomberg News reviewed. For Boston-based Flywire, tighter immigration rules could make it harder to hire the engineers who build its payments technology systems. The company, which handles billions of dollars in payments a month for colleges and other clients, said in a quarterly filing this month that it is considering “reallocating hiring and development activities to lower-cost jurisdictions where we already operate” to offset increases in H-1B visa costs. It warned that trouble recruiting and retaining specialists could slow its own product development, while fewer foreign students choosing American universities would mean less tuition money moving through its network. Data is beginning to show the impact of Trump’s limits. During the 2025 budget year, which included the last three full months of the Biden administration, the US issued about 260,000 fewer temporary, non-immigrant visas than the prior year, according to federal visa data analyzed by the Migration Policy Institute. International enrollment at US universities has declined, with an estimated 15% drop in new foreign students this fall, according to the Institute of International Education. Participation in Optional Practical Training, which gives international students temporary work authorization, dropped by 6% at the start of the 2026-27 academic year, marking the first decline in five years. Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart in Denver, said his corporate clients are asking about the risks they face if they choose to hire foreigners. For many of them, the thinking is “we know we’re doing oversight right, we know we are compliant with the law, but the concern is if we get charged anyway,” he said. He added that many clients fear that any perceived slip-up could prompt the government to ban them from work visa programs or launch criminal probes.  And over the long term, he said, some of his corporate clients are wondering if it’s worth the hassle of trying to navigate an increasingly complex employer-based immigration landscape. “Some are saying it’s too much, it’s time to start offshoring,” Thomas said. While legal challenges could limit the scope of Trump’s restrictions, Thomas and others said that the perception that the administration is making the US less welcoming has already broken through. “It creates this profound instability for the entire immigration ecosystem,” said Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association. “We are creating a brain drain.”

item.content:encoded:
Home / India News / Cyclone Akvan disrupts air traffic, 20 flights cancelled in Ranchi

Cyclone Akvan disrupts air traffic, 20 flights cancelled in Ranchi Visibility at Birsa Munda Airport remained around 1,000 metres until 1 pm, below the 1,200-1,500 metres required for safe take-offs and landings, an airport official said

Children walk along the shore ahead of the expected landfall of Cyclone Akvan in Aryapalli, Odisha, India, November 20 | REUTERS

Press Trust of India Ranchi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 4:25 PM IST

Listen to This Article

As many as 20 flights were cancelled at the Birsa Munda Airport here on Saturday due to inclement weather triggered by cyclone 'Akvan', an official said. Jharkhand has been experiencing cloudy weather coupled with light rain since Friday under the influence of the cyclone. For safe landing or take-off, a visibility between 1,200 and 1,500 metres is required. "The visibility at Ranchi airport was around 1,000 metres until 1pm," Airport Director Vinod Kumar told PTI. In all, 20 scheduled flights were cancelled due to bad weather, including six Air India Express flights, an airport official said. Also Read

Cyclone Akvan: Odisha's Mayurbhanj, Balasore under red alert for heavy rain

Cyclone Akvan crosses Odisha coast, brings heavy rain; no damage reported

In addition, four flights were diverted due to inclement weather.

The state's weather is likely to improve from Sunday with clearing of clouds, an IMD official said. "We are expecting the weather to improve from Sunday with dense fog in the morning hours. A clear sunshine is likely from November 23," Baburaj PP, director at Ranchi Meteorological Centre, told PTI. Chaibasa Sadar in West Singbhum district recorded highest rainfall at 34.4 mm during the past 24 hours till 8.30am on Saturday. Ghatsila in East Singhbhum district registered 32.6 mm rainfall, Simega 28.2mm, Jamshedpur 22.2 mm and Ranchi recorded 12.4 mm rainfall. The maximum temperature is likely to remain unchanged for the next 24 hours in the state and thereafter it will start rising by 6 degree Celsius during the next three days, according to the weather bulletin.

Similarly, the minimum temperature is likely to drop by 5 degree Celsius over the next two days, it stated. Ranchi registered a minimum temperature at 17.5 degree Celsius, 4.4 notches above the normal, while Jamshedpur recorded minimum at 19.6 degree Celsius and Daltonganj at 19.8 degree Celsius on Saturday.

item.description: Announced at the institute's 75th anniversary celebrations, the funding will support advanced AI research, educational opportunities and capacity building for students and researchers ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Technology / Tech News / Google announces $5 mn funding for IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research

Google announces $5 mn funding for IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research Announced at the institute's 75th anniversary celebrations, the funding will support advanced AI research, educational opportunities and capacity building for students and researchers

As part of educational opportunities, it will support expansion of AI training and curriculum development for students and faculty (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 2:01 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Technology giant Google on Saturday said it will provide IIT Kharagpur with $5 million, about ₹46 crore, to develop and accelerate advanced AI research. Speaking on the 75th anniversary of IIT Kharagpur, Director Suman Chakraborty said that the fund support for applied AI research has been envisaged by the institute's alumnus and Google CEO Sundar Pichai. "Google is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million in funding to help develop and accelerate advanced AI research, while cultivating India's next generation of scientific and technical talent," the company said in a blog. The funding will support the institute's researchers and students across three core pillars, comprising advanced AI research, educational opportunities and AI capacity building.

Under advanced AI research, the fund will support tackling critical, real-world challenges by deploying AI for Indic languages, materials science, agriculture, and educational technology. Also Read

India has shown it can break limits, unlock possibilities: PM Modi

As part of educational opportunities, it will support expansion of AI training and curriculum development for students and faculty. The fund will support the institute's AI frameworks and tooling to elevate the technological ecosystem across the campus. "IIT Kharagpur is driving groundbreaking work in areas like Indic languages, agriculture, and education, and Google is excited to help accelerate this impact with a new partnership. Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own," Pichai said.

He said India is increasingly at the forefront of innovation; programmes like this will help implement Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision that the benefits of AI reach everyone in India.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: TrueRE Oriana Power to invest ₹750 crore in five compressed biogas projects
item.description: The renewable energy firm plans to establish five CBG plants with a combined capacity of 110 tonnes per day across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat over the next two years.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / TrueRE Oriana Power to invest ₹750 crore in five compressed biogas projects

TrueRE Oriana Power to invest ₹750 crore in five compressed biogas projects The renewable energy firm plans to establish five CBG plants with a combined capacity of 110 tonnes per day across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat over the next two years.

TrueRE Oriana Power plans to invest ₹750 crore in five compressed biogas projects | Image: Bloomberg

Sudheer Pal Singh New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 6:55 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Renewable energy platform TrueRE Oriana Power announced that it will set up five compressed biogas (CBG) projects with a combined production capacity of 110 tonnes per day (TPD) at an investment of ₹750 crore.   The company has already registered and obtained approvals under the GOBARdhan scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, and the five plants will be set up in Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat within the next two years.   These plants will strengthen the company’s presence in the green fuels segment as part of its strategy to build a diversified clean energy portfolio spanning generation, storage and consumption, it said.

"We view alternative fuels like green hydrogen, ammonia, and CBG as high potential emerging opportunities. In the next few years, we will continue to invest strategically to further increase our total production capacity,” said Rupal Gupta, managing director and chief executive officer, TrueRE Oriana Power.   The company has already delivered two projects with a capacity of 21 TPD each in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra. Beyond CBG, it is also advancing its presence in green hydrogen and its derivatives. Also Read

Scaling up CBG may save India $20 bn a year in LNG imports by 2030: Report

Reliance plans to invest about $1.6 billion to build new biogas plants

It has secured a 10,000-tonne-per-annum green hydrogen production award under the Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) programme and a separate award for the production and supply of 60,000 metric tonnes per annum of green ammonia. The green ammonia project has progressed through land identification and preliminary front-end engineering and design activities.

The company recently won the largest allocation in Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company's 2,000-megawatt/4,000-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery storage tender. With this win, the company’s total battery energy storage system (BESS) portfolio stands at 2.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh), with an additional pipeline of 4 GWh.   By 2030, the company is targeting 6 gigawatts (GW) of solar engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) capacity, 2.5 GW of solar independent power producer (IPP) capacity, 20 GWh of BESS capacity and 1 million tonnes per annum of e-fuels capacity.   More From This Section
